summary.text: The imaginary unit, written i, is a solution to x² = −1, which no real number solves.
Any real-number multiple of it is called an imaginary number, and combining it with the real numbers through addition and multiplication builds the complex numbers.
Electrical engineers usually write it as j instead, because the letter i is commonly used for electric current.

facts.label: Square roots of −1
facts.value: There are two: i and its additive inverse −i

facts.label: Origin of names
facts.value: Imaginary is credited to Descartes; the i notation comes from Euler

facts.label: Place on the plane
facts.value: One unit from the origin along the imaginary axis

items.prompt: A student insists that only one number can be multiplied by itself to give −1. Among the complex numbers, how many such numbers are there?

options.label: Just one, the imaginary unit
Two, the imaginary unit and its negative
None, since no real number works
Infinitely many, one for each angle

items.explain: The number −1 has two distinct complex square roots, i and −i.

items.prompt: An electrical engineer's notes use the letter j for √(−1). Why avoid the usual letter?

options.label: It is reserved for counting turns of wire in a coil
It looks too much like the digit one on a page
It already means a negative number in circuits
It is already the usual symbol for electric current

items.explain: In electrical engineering the imaginary unit is written j because i is commonly used to denote electric current.

items.prompt: Why did early mathematicians call the square roots of negative numbers imaginary?

options.label: Only numbers from measurement or basic arithmetic counted as numbers then
They were proved false and kept only as a handy trick
They were smaller than every real number
They could not be added or multiplied

items.explain: In early-modern mathematics only what are now called real numbers were considered numbers at all, so the square root of a negative number seemed undefined or nonsensical.

items.prompt: A calculation produces the term 5i². Treating i as an unknown and using its definition, what does that term become?

options.label: 5, since squaring undoes the i
5i, since only one i is removed
−5, since i² is replaced by −1
−5i, since the sign moves to the i

items.explain: The definition lets any occurrence of i² be replaced with −1, so 5i² becomes −5.

items.prompt: Draw the complex plane with the real numbers along a left-to-right line. Where would you mark the imaginary unit?

options.label: One unit from the origin, along the perpendicular vertical axis
One unit to the right of the origin, on the real line
At the origin itself, because it is not a real number
One unit from the origin, along the diagonal

items.explain: The imaginary unit is the point one unit from the origin along the imaginary axis, which is drawn vertically, perpendicular to the real axis.

items.prompt: The two square roots of −1 share every property. Is there a built-in reason to call one of them i and the other −i?

options.label: Yes, i is the positive one, just like positive real numbers
No, which is which is a choice, since nothing tells them apart
Yes, the one that sits higher on the plane gets the plus sign
No, because the two are in fact exactly the same number

items.explain: The two solutions are distinct numbers, but no property of one is missing from the other, so it is inherently ambiguous which is which. Neither is positive or negative the way real numbers are.
